asSun.p: Saturn rules Capricorn, and The Devil is Capricorn's Major, so a Capricorn Sun gets this card whether it likes it or not. Most people flinch when they hear that, and I understand why, but have a proper look at the picture first. Two people are chained to a block, and the chains are hanging so loosely that either of them could lift theirs off over their head in a second. Nobody's forcing anybody. For a sign that takes on as much as Capricorn does, that's a useful thing to be shown. The Sun has no special dignity in Capricorn. It's a visitor in Saturn's house and it picks up Saturn's habits, so your sense of who you are gets built out of time, effort, results and what you've got to show for the years. Capricorn is cardinal earth as well, which means you're the one who starts the practical thing, the business, the savings plan, the renovation, and then carries it for a decade.

Mostly it lives in the word 'should'. You wake up with a list already running. On a Friday night you're still answering the email that could have waited, because leaving it feels worse than doing it. The family group chat asks who's sorting Christmas and you've quietly booked the place already. Someone at work says you did a great job and you reply by listing the three things still outstanding. You've had some version of a five-year plan since school, and you've mostly stuck to it. None of this feels like a chain from the inside. It feels like being a grown-up, and you've been one since you were about eleven. That's Saturn colouring the Sun, and it's why you rarely feel you've arrived. There's always one more thing to finish before you're allowed to be pleased with yourself.

You can see what other people are tied to, and you don't judge them for it. A friend admits they're in debt, or drinking every night, or still sleeping with the ex, and you don't do the shocked face. You ask how much, how often, and what the plan is. I've seen a Capricorn Sun sit at a kitchen table with a friend's credit card statements for three hours, sorting them into piles, and the friend walked out with a way through it and no shame. That's rare. Most people either lecture or look away. You also understand that pleasure is allowed, which surprises people who've only seen the work side of you. When you finally take the afternoon off you take it properly, good food, a long bath, a nap, and the phone in another room.

The chain on this card runs both ways, and the less obvious one is the chain other people wear to you. You make yourself necessary. You're the one who knows the passwords to the family accounts, who holds the spare keys, who understands the mortgage, and nobody else is ever quite shown how it works. That feels like looking after people. Some of it is. Some of it is control, and a way of making sure you're never left. The other thing is that you'll trade a lot of your own life for status without noticing the price going up. The promotion that means you miss every school pickup. The house that needs both incomes forever. You'll tell yourself it's for later, when the kids are older or the loan's paid off. Once a year, get a calendar out and check whether that date has moved.

When something goes wrong your first move is to tighten everything. A job loss, a diagnosis in the family, a month where the bills land all at once, and within a day you've got a spreadsheet, a budget, a plan with dates. People are grateful for about a week. Then the tightening carries on past where it helps. You get curt, you cut the small pleasures from everybody's life including your own, and the one habit you allow yourself, the second glass, the late-night scrolling, the extra hour at the desk, quietly gets bigger. Your household ends up feeling rationed and slightly told off. What actually helps is handing one real task to someone else and letting them do it badly. Then sleep, and something that makes you laugh out loud, ideally with other people in the room.

You want to be proud of what the two of you are building. A house, a family, a life that looks solid from the street and is solid inside too. I've seen a lot of Capricorn Suns pick a partner the way they'd pick a business partner, reliable, ambitious, good with money, and to be honest it often works better than the romantic version. What people don't expect is how physical you are. Under all the reserve there's an earth sign, and it likes touch, a proper bed and no hurry in the morning. The trouble spot is staying because you committed, long after it stopped feeling good. You're loyal to promises, and leaving would feel like failing at something, which a Capricorn Sun takes personally. Ask yourself once in a while whether you're still choosing this or just keeping your word.

Capricorn's natural house is the tenth, the public role and the reputation, so work isn't a side matter for you. It's where you find out who you are. You want your name on the door eventually, and you'll put in fifteen years to get it there. You're fair, you don't panic, and staff trust you because you do what you said you'd do. The Devil's catch for a Capricorn Sun is that the job title starts standing in for you. Someone at a barbecue asks what you do and that's the whole answer. A restructure hits you harder than it would most people, and even a long holiday can leave you a bit lost by the second week. Keep one thing in your week that has nothing to do with work and that you're not trying to get good at.

Capricorns are often said to get younger as they go, and in my experience that's broadly true. At twenty a Capricorn Sun tends to be serious, old for their age, a bit tight with money and very tight with feelings, already worried about the future while friends are out. Pleasure feels like something you haven't earned yet. The mid-thirties are usually the decade of the climb, and it's also when the handcuffs go on, the mortgage, the title, the life that has to be kept running. The fifties are where a lot of Capricorns finally loosen up. The status has either come or stopped mattering, and there's often a real outbreak of fun, travel, a late hobby, a sense of humour people didn't know you had. The ones who don't are often still keeping the same hours at sixty-five, mostly out of habit.

Write down every regular 'have to' in your week, the calls, the favours, the standing commitments. Next to each one, write who would actually notice if you stopped. Pick the one where the honest answer is nobody, or only you, and drop it for a month. Put something you enjoy in that slot instead, and don't use it to catch up on work.

asMoon.p: The Moon is in detriment in Capricorn. That's the technical word for a planet sitting in the sign opposite its home, and the Moon's home is Cancer, so in Capricorn it's about as far from its natural habits as it gets. It still does its job, but it's working against the grain, and the people close to you can usually tell. Where a Cancer Moon feels first and sorts it out later, yours tends to sort it out first and then feel it, sometimes months on, sometimes in the car. Capricorn is Saturn's earth sign, cardinal, practical, so the feelings get handled like a job. The Devil is Capricorn's card, and as a Moon card it isn't about ambition at all. The two people on the block aren't pulling at their chains at all. That's closer to the Moon's business, the comfort you've got used to and stopped seeing.

You feel safe when things are in order and money's in the account. A full fridge and a paid bill do more for your nerves than a hug, most days, and you might be a bit embarrassed to admit that. You eat standing up at the bench. When a friend rings in tears you catch yourself thinking of solutions while they're still in the middle of the story. A Sunday with nothing to do makes you restless by mid-morning, so you clean out a cupboard. Rest has to be earned, and the reward for a hard week is usually something small and familiar, the same takeaway, the same show, the same drink, and you'd feel oddly cheated without it. You also carry old family duties in your body. A phone call from a parent can have your shoulders up round your ears inside a minute.

Your feelings are reliable. That sounds like faint praise and it really isn't. People know where they stand with a Capricorn Moon, and they know that if you say you'll come, you come, at two in the morning if that's when the car broke down. When everyone else at the hospital is falling apart you're the one who's found the parking, the forms and the vending machine that works, and nobody had to ask you. There's another gift under that. Because the Moon has to work hard in this sign, you've learnt a lot about your own moods by necessity. You can sit next to someone else's craving or grief and not be frightened by it, because you've watched your own from quite close up and it didn't finish you.

The comfort habits are the obvious bit. The less obvious bit is how you ration comfort for other people too. You can be quietly stingy with warmth, the same way some people are stingy with money, as if there's only so much and it has to last. Your partner's upset about something small and you point out, reasonably, that it's small. Your kid wants a cuddle when you're in the middle of the tax return and gets told in a minute. There's often an old rule behind it, picked up early, that needing things is weak and being looked after has to be paid back. You probably don't believe that when you say it out loud. Your body still acts on it. And when you need something yourself you tend to go very quiet about it, then feel hurt that nobody guessed.

Stress goes straight into routine. Something awful happens, a breakup, a death, a friend who lets you down badly, and the first thing you do is keep going to work. You're quietly proud of that. You tidy, you cook in batches, you stay up late getting ahead. About a week in, the body starts collecting. Your jaw aches, your sleep goes thin, and the evening treat turns into two, then into most evenings. The people around you say you're coping brilliantly, which makes it harder to say you aren't. Your partner feels shut out and a bit useless. What helps is permission more than advice. Someone telling you to stop, and then actually taking the kids or the dinner off you, and you letting them. A good cry would help too, and it'll usually come on its own schedule.

You need to know a relationship is going to last before you let it get soft, which means the early months can feel a bit like a probation period for both of you. Once you're in, you're in for good, and the love comes out as provision. The car's serviced, the bills are paid, the flights are booked. Try to notice when your partner wants the warmth itself and not the service. The Moon's own sign, Cancer, is your opposite, so you're often drawn to people who cry easily, cook for the whole street and say what they feel on the day they feel it. They can unsettle you. They're also good for you. The pattern to watch is getting used to a relationship that feels cold, because cold is what you're used to, and calling that stability.

Work is where your nerves feel safest, which is exactly why it can take over. A clear task, a deadline, a bit of recognition from someone serious, and you feel steady in a way home doesn't always manage. You're the colleague who stays calm in the audit and who notices the numbers don't add up. The risk is work becoming your comfort habit, the thing you reach for when you're upset the way someone else reaches for a drink. It's a respectable one, so nobody stops you. I'd keep an eye on how you feel on the first morning of a holiday. If it's a kind of dread, work has become where you hide. Look for a job that pays fairly and lets you leave at a fixed hour. You'll do better in it than you think.

At twenty a Capricorn Moon has often been the responsible one at home for years already, a parent who leant on you, a family where money was tight, a childhood with a lot of chores in it. Feelings get put off until there's time. By the mid-thirties the self-reliance has paid off, a career, a home, some savings, and there's often a first real crack, a burnout or a relationship that ends because you weren't there, when the backlog comes due. That can be the making of you. The fifties are, in my experience, kind to this Moon. You've usually learnt that rest doesn't have to be earned. There's often an ageing parent to look after by then, and you do it well, with less resentment than you'd have guessed. The harder part is letting someone look after you.

Pick one comfort you reach for without thinking, the evening glass, the phone in bed, the extra hour of work. For one week, before you reach for it, sit down for two minutes and name out loud what you're actually feeling. Tired, lonely, cross, whatever it is. Then have the thing or don't, either's fine. The two minutes are the practice.

asRising.p: Your rising sign is whatever was coming over the eastern horizon when you were born, and it sets the first house, which is the body, the face and the way you go into things. With Capricorn rising, Saturn becomes your chart ruler, which means the planet of time, limits and slow effort is running the whole show from the front door. The Devil is Capricorn's card, so it's the one people meet first. The horned figure on the card sits very still above everyone else, watching. There's a stillness to Capricorn rising too, a watchful quality that other people read as authority long before you've said a word. The sign is cardinal earth, so you do start things, you just start them with a budget. You walk into a situation and you're already working out what it'll cost, who's in charge and where the exit is.

People assume you're in charge. At a party someone asks you where the bathroom is even though it isn't your house. In a new job you get asked for sign-off in the first week. You've probably been told you look serious when you were just thinking, and strangers can find you a bit intimidating until you crack a very dry joke and they realise you've been quietly enjoying yourself the whole time. You dress well, or at least properly, and you notice straight away when someone's shoes are cheap. In a first meeting you listen more than you speak, because you want to know what the deal is before you commit. The first house is the body as well, and with Saturn running it you tend to hold yourself a bit braced, shoulders set, even when you're perfectly relaxed.

You can read what's going on in a room, and especially who holds the power and who's hooked on what. In a negotiation you notice the person who needs the deal more. At a family gathering you spot which relative everyone's quietly afraid of within twenty minutes. That's useful, and you use it with more restraint than people expect. There's also a steadiness at the front of you that makes people behave. A rowdy meeting gets quieter when you sit down. A kid who's pushing limits with everyone else will usually test you once and then stop. First meetings with difficult people come easier to you than to most, the bank manager, the ex's new partner, the landlord who's been ignoring your emails. You don't need them to like you, they can tell, and so they're straight with you.

The guarded front turns into a cage of its own if you let it. You get so used to being the composed one that you can't find the way to be anything else in public, even when you want to. Your friends see a joke, a raised eyebrow, a well-managed evening, and they don't see that you went home and lay on the floor for an hour. There's a cynical streak here too. Because your instinct looks for the angle, you can assume everyone has one. Someone does something kind for you and you spend a day working out what they want. Now and again that's accurate. Mostly it isn't, and it costs you the kind of friendships that start with someone being generous for no reason.

Pressure makes the face harder, and you get quicker to cut people off, the friend who rings at the wrong moment, the colleague who wants to talk it through. A crisis at work and you're immediately calm, formal, a bit cold, and people either find that reassuring or frightening. You go into problem-solving and you don't let anyone see a wobble. A week later it's in the body. A stiff neck, a tooth that aches, a back that goes when you pick up the shopping. You keep turning up and looking fine, so the people around you don't know to offer anything, and then they're hurt to find out afterwards what you were carrying. What helps is physical. A massage, a long walk, a heat pack, and one person you can drop the manners with.

With Capricorn on the first house, Cancer falls on your seventh, the house of partners. So the people who get under your guard tend to be warm, domestic, emotional, the kind who ask how your day really was and wait for the answer. You might find that a bit much at first, and then find you can't do without it. Early on you're careful, and potential partners can read that as disinterest. It's worth saying something warm on purpose, sooner than feels natural. Aries sits on your fourth house, the home, so behind closed doors you're a lot more fiery and impatient than your public manner suggests, and whoever lives with you gets that version. They should know they've been let in, because from where they're standing it can just look like temper.

People trust you with responsibility on sight, which is a real advantage in interviews and a real risk once you're hired, because you get handed everything. Libra sits on your tenth house, career, which softens the picture. The work that suits you usually involves fairness, relationships, taste or judgement, law, design, mediation, HR, anything where you have to be pleasant and firm in the same breath. You're good at telling someone no in a way they thank you for. The Devil at the front of your chart also means you can see how a workplace keeps people stuck, the bonus that's always next year, the manager who plays favourites. Use that to look after your team, and say something the first time you see it being done to someone junior.

Capricorn rising at twenty often looks thirty-five. You're taken seriously early, handed responsibility early, and quite often you're lonely inside it because people your age find you a bit reserved. By the mid-thirties the face and the age start to line up, and it's usually a good decade, the thing people trusted you with at twenty-two turns into real authority. The risk then is getting so identified with the composed front that you forget there was a person underneath who liked being silly. The fifties tend to bring a looser Capricorn rising. You've usually stopped caring what the room thinks, you'll wear the odd thing and say the odd thing, and the body wants proper upkeep, the physio, the dentist, a decent chair. A lot of people with this rising look better at sixty than they did at twenty-five.

Next time you meet someone new, a colleague, a friend's partner, the parent at pickup, tell them one small true thing about yourself in the first five minutes that isn't about work. That you're bad at parallel parking, that you hate coriander, that you're tired. Watch what it does to the conversation. Try it three times this month and notice who relaxes.

asBirthCard.p: This one comes from your birthdate, not from anything in your chart. Add up every digit of the date, and if the total goes over 22 add those digits again, and yours lands on fifteen, which is The Devil. It says nothing about your Sun sign. Fifteen is built from one and five, and one and five make six, which is The Lovers, so the card carries a choice inside it. In fact the two cards look alike. Two people standing side by side, a figure above them, and on The Devil they've got chains on. Fifteen comes right after Temperance, the card of mixing things slowly and in the right amount, and right before The Tower, where the building comes down. It's the card where the mixing has gone too far and nobody's knocked anything over yet. The card's own sign is Capricorn, earthy and Saturn-ruled, so its business is solid things, money, bodies, work and time.

As a pattern across a life, fifteen tends to show up as bargains. Over and over you find yourself in some kind of deal where you get something you want and pay for it with something you didn't quite price. The flat you could afford because it was forty minutes further out. The job that paid well because it asked for your evenings. The friendship that's great fun as long as you're the one who pays. The family role you picked up at fourteen and are still doing at forty, the one who keeps the peace at every birthday lunch. None of these is a disaster, and most of them were reasonable at the time. The pattern is that you often don't notice the deal until years into it, and the moment of noticing is where things move.

Living with that pattern makes you very hard to fool. You get to know what a hook looks like. A salesperson, a charming new manager, a relative who's about to ask for money, you see it coming a mile off, and you're usually kind about it. You also know how to get out of a deal decently, because you've had to. You've broken a lease, left a job, stepped off a committee, and nobody ended up hating you. There's a practical gift too. Because the card belongs to earth, the people with this birth number often get good at money and bodies, at knowing what things actually cost and what a body actually needs. You're the one who can tell a friend their business idea is lovely and won't pay, and they listen, because you're obviously on their side.

The hard version of fifteen is loyalty to a bad deal. You've put so much into something, a relationship, a career, a house, a way of seeing yourself, that walking away feels like admitting you were wrong about half your life. So you stay, and you get very good at explaining why. The other shadow is quieter. You can be drawn to intense people, the ones with a bit of danger or a big appetite, and end up in the role of the sensible one who holds everything together while they have the fun. At a party you're the one who drives everyone home. On the group holiday you're the one holding the passports and the booking codes. There's a resentment that builds from that, slowly, and it tends to come out sideways.

Under strain a fifteen pattern reaches for the familiar thing, and often it's a thing you'd sworn off. The ex you text after a bad week, the old job you consider going back to, the habit that crept back in during the move. It feels like relief for about three days. A week later there's the shame, and the shame is usually worse than the thing itself, because now you're hiding it as well. The people around you notice you've gone secretive and can't work out why. What helps is saying it plainly to one person you trust, early, before the story hardens into a secret. And a proper look at the practical side, the sleep, the money, the loneliness, because those are usually what the old habit was covering for.

Love with this number has a lot of heat in it, and the pattern tends to be intensity first and clarity later. You fall for chemistry and figure out the compatibility afterwards, and some of that is a lot of fun. The less obvious thing is how easily you take on the terms of the other person's life. Their friends, their schedule, their family's way of arguing, and after a year you're not sure which of your habits are yours. Since fifteen carries six inside it, every relationship eventually comes back round to a choice. It's a real one, even when it's about something as dull as whose town you'll live in. The partners who suit you are the secure ones, happy for you to keep your own friends and your own nights out.

People with this birth card often do well in work that deals with appetite, money or power, and deals with them honestly. Finance, addiction work, sales, hospitality, law, therapy, anything where you need to understand what people want and what it's costing them. You're unusually good at spotting the trap in a contract or the catch in an offer. The pattern to watch is the bargain again, the job that pays you a bit too well to leave. I've seen plenty of people with this card stay ten years in a role they'd outgrown in three, because the money and the title had become the whole point. Keep a note on your phone of what you'd do if every job paid the same, and read it back whenever a pay rise is on the table.

In your twenties the fifteen pattern mostly looks like appetite. Big loves, big nights, some debt, a few deals you didn't read properly, and a sense that nothing is permanent yet. By the mid-thirties the deals have set. There's a mortgage, a career, a relationship, obligations with real weight, and this is usually the decade when a person with this card first notices that some of the chains were optional. It can be uncomfortable. It's also where the life starts to become yours on purpose. The fifties tend to bring a kind of hard-earned freedom. People with this number often end up lighter in their later years, having put down the roles and habits they finally saw clearly, and they're often very good company, with a lot of stories and no interest in judging anyone else's.

Pick one commitment in your life you've never really questioned, a subscription, a standing favour, a role in the family. Write two lines on paper. What you get from it, and what it costs you, in money, time or mood. Don't decide anything yet. Just leave the paper somewhere you'll see it for a week, and notice whether your answer to the second line changes.
